case.case_title: Gooneratne and Others v. Chandrananda De Silva, Commissioner of Elections
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 49/87, decided on 27 August 1987

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the refusal by the Commissioner of Elections to register the Eksath Lanka Janatha Pakshaya (ELJP) as a recognised political party violated the fundamental right to equality under Article 12(1) of the Constitution by discriminating against the party compared to other parties similarly situated.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioners argued that the refusal to recognise ELJP was unjust, unfair, unreasonable, and discriminatory, violating their fundamental right to equality under Article 12(1). They contended that the Commissioner applied an improper and inconsistent standard, giving undue weight to the party's short existence and requiring recognition by other parties, which was not legally necessary.
case_context.respondent_argument: The Commissioner of Elections argued that ELJP was not sufficiently organised or established to contest elections, was in an incipient stage, and that recognition required a degree of existence, growth, and political acceptance. He relied on subjective satisfaction under section 7(5) of the Parliamentary Elections Act and emphasized the party's infancy and lack of recognition by other political parties.
key_facts: ELJP was formed in January 1987 with a constitution, office bearers, and over 10,000 members.
The Commissioner refused recognition on 31 March 1987, citing the party's infancy and insufficient organisation.
Other parties with less material, such as Sri Lanka Mahajana Pakshaya, were granted recognition despite similar infancy.
The Commissioner applied different criteria to ELJP compared to other parties, especially regarding the time factor and recognition by other parties.
The petitioners challenged the refusal as patent unreasonableness and discrimination under Article 12(1).

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that Article 12(1) prohibits discrimination between persons or entities who are substantially similarly circumstanced. The Commissioner must apply consistent criteria and not discriminate by applying different standards to similarly situated parties. The subjective satisfaction required by the statute is reviewable for patent unreasonableness and legal error. The Commissioner erred by giving undue weight to the party's short existence and requiring recognition by other parties, which is not a legal prerequisite.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The court found that ELJP had the fundamental attributes of a political party organised to contest elections, including a constitution, membership, organisation, and political programme. The Commissioner misdirected himself by focusing excessively on the party's infancy and by requiring recognition by other parties. The Commissioner applied a more stringent standard to ELJP than to other parties, resulting in unjustified discrimination. This violated the petitioners' right to equality under Article 12(1).
principles_established: Article 12(1) guarantees equality before the law and prohibits discrimination between similarly situated persons or entities.
Subjective decisions by public officials are subject to judicial review for patent unreasonableness and legal error.
Recognition as a political party does not require a minimum period of existence or recognition by other parties.
Public officials must apply consistent criteria and not discriminate between similarly situated applicants.
precedents_cited: Secretary of State for Education v. Tameside Metropolitan Borough [1976] 3 All ER 663
Associated Provincial Picture House Ltd. v. Wednesbury Corporation [1947] 2 All ER 680
Anisminic Ltd. v. Foreign Compensation Commission [1969] 1 All ER 208
Re Racal Communications Ltd. [1980] 2 All ER 634

outcome.holding: The court allowed the application, set aside the Commissioner's refusal order, and directed the Commissioner to register ELJP as a recognised political party. The court held that the refusal violated Article 12(1) by discriminating against ELJP and applying an improper standard.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The Commissioner of Elections was directed to grant the petitioners' application for registration of ELJP as a recognised political party and to make other relevant consequential orders.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the court's reasoning because the petitioners claimed that the refusal to recognise their party was discriminatory compared to other parties similarly situated. The court's decision rested on the principle of equality before the law and equal protection, finding that the Commissioner had applied inconsistent and discriminatory criteria.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The court found that the Commissioner gave undue weight to the party's infancy and required recognition by other parties, which is not necessary under the law, resulting in discrimination violating Article 12(1). The court noted that other parties with less material were recognised, showing inconsistent treatment.
